title: Scrotal exploration with bilateral orchidopexy
subtitle: Untwist, judge viability, fix both sides

sources.org: European Association of Urology (EAU) and European Society for Paediatric Urology (ESPU)
sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology: acute scrotum in children

indications: Suspected testicular torsion. Exploration is the diagnostic test as well as the treatment.
Acute scrotum where torsion cannot be excluded clinically or on imaging.
Intermittent torsion with a typical history: elective bilateral fixation.
contraindications: None that justify delay in suspected torsion. Anaesthetic risk is managed, not used as a reason to wait.
Confirmed epididymo-orchitis or torsion of an appendix testis with torsion confidently excluded.
preparation: Document the time of onset of pain and the time of decision to operate.
Consent for exploration, detorsion, fixation of both testes, and possible orchidectomy. In a minor, involve the parents and the young person; discuss the possibility of losing the testis honestly.
Nil by mouth status is not a reason to delay; discuss with the anaesthetist.
positioning: Supine with the legs slightly abducted; the penis taped up onto the abdomen.
equipment: Minor general set with fine dissecting instruments; bipolar diathermy.
Sutures for fixation per surgeon preference and for layered closure.
anatomy: The tunica vaginalis normally attaches to the posterior testis. A high attachment (the bell-clapper deformity) lets the testis rotate inside it, and it is usually bilateral.
The spermatic cord contains the testicular artery, the pampiniform plexus and the vas deferens; torsion twists all of them.
The median raphe allows access to both hemiscrota through one incision; transverse incisions over each side are an alternative.
The appendix testis lies at the upper pole and may twist on its own, mimicking torsion.
criticalSafety: Do not delay theatre for investigations when torsion is clinically likely.
Always assess viability after detorsion and warming before deciding on fixation or orchidectomy.
Always fix the contralateral testis in confirmed torsion: the anatomical predisposition is usually bilateral.
commonErrors: Waiting for an ultrasound or a morning list.
Removing a dusky testis without allowing time to reperfuse after detorsion and warming.
Fixing the torted side and forgetting the other.
Placing fixation sutures through the epididymis or vessels.
complications: Testicular atrophy despite detorsion, particularly after long ischaemia.
Orchidectomy and its psychological impact; later prosthesis discussion.
Recurrent torsion if fixation is inadequate.
postop: Day-case or overnight stay; scrotal support and simple analgesia.
Explain the findings to the patient and family, including the risk of later atrophy.
Follow up to examine testicular size; discuss a testicular prosthesis after orchidectomy when appropriate.

steps.emphasis: Record the time of onset of pain and the consent for bilateral fixation and possible orchidectomy.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely needed for clean scrotal surgery; follow local policy.
Supine, penis taped up. This is a short operation; do not let positioning delay the incision.
Scrotal haematoma is the commonest complication. Use bipolar diathermy on the dartos edges.
Only if an orchidectomy or appendix testis excision was performed.
Close the dartos and the skin in layers with absorbable sutures.

step.scrot.incision.title: Scrotal incision and opening the tunica vaginalis
step.scrot.incision.why: A midline raphe incision reaches both testes through one wound, which matters because both sides will be fixed.
how: Incise along the median raphe, or transversely over the affected hemiscrotum.
Divide the dartos and open the tunica vaginalis of the affected side; note the colour of any hydrocele fluid (blood-stained suggests torsion).
Deliver the testis into the wound.
pitfalls: An incision too small to deliver the testis comfortably.

step.scrot.detort.title: Identify torsion and detort
step.scrot.detort.why: Restoring flow is the whole purpose of the operation. Every minute counts and nothing else is done until the cord is untwisted.
how: Identify the twist in the cord, count the turns, and note the direction.
Untwist the cord fully, until the cord lies straight and the epididymis is in its normal posterior position.
If no torsion is found, look for a twisted appendix testis or other pathology and remove a torted appendage.
pitfalls: Incomplete detorsion because the number of turns was not counted.

step.scrot.viability.title: Assess viability after warming
step.scrot.viability.why: A testis that looks black on delivery often recovers colour after detorsion. Deciding too early removes testes that could have been saved.
how: Wrap the testis in warm saline swabs and wait several minutes while the other side is explored.
Reassess colour, and if doubt remains, make a small incision in the tunica albuginea and observe for fresh arterial bleeding.
Decide with a senior: fix a testis that bleeds and pinks up; remove one that is clearly necrotic.
pitfalls: Orchidectomy on first sight of a dark testis.
Keeping a frankly necrotic testis out of reluctance to remove it.

step.scrot.orchidectomy.title: Orchidectomy for a non-viable testis
step.scrot.orchidectomy.why: A dead testis left in place risks infection and prolonged pain. Removing it is the right outcome when viability is clearly lost, not a failure.
how: Transfix and ligate the spermatic cord in two places above the necrotic tissue, separately ligating the vas if preferred.
Remove the testis and send it for histology.
Record the decision, the findings and who agreed it in the operative note.
pitfalls: A single ligature on a thick oedematous cord that slips and bleeds into the scrotum.

step.scrot.fixation.title: Fixation of the affected testis
step.scrot.fixation.why: The bell-clapper anatomy that allowed the torsion is still there after detorsion. Fixation prevents the testis rotating again.
how: Fix the testis to the scrotal wall by sutures through the tunica albuginea at several points, or by placing it in a dartos pouch, per surgeon practice.
Avoid the epididymis and the vessels; place sutures superficially in the tunica albuginea.
Check that the cord lies straight and untwisted after fixation.
pitfalls: Deep sutures into the testicular parenchyma.

step.scrot.contralateral.title: Contralateral fixation
step.scrot.contralateral.why: The anatomical predisposition is usually bilateral. A boy who loses one testis to torsion and later loses the other is left anorchic.
how: Open the contralateral tunica vaginalis through the same midline incision or a separate one.
Fix the contralateral testis by the same method.
Document the contralateral anatomy (bell-clapper or not) in the note.
pitfalls: Omitting it because the operation went well on the affected side.
